main.job: identity: what or who something is, origin, profession, lasting traits
main.why: one of the two ways Spanish says 'be'; ser/estar is the #1 trap for English speakers

main.job: location and current state (where something is, how someone is right now)
main.why: the other 'be'; only the estar + gerundio pattern is known, not estar's own location/state job (R-EX-03)
the existence building block; English speakers reach for 'está' instead

main.job: have: possession, age, and states like hunger or cold (tener hambre)
main.why: have-job building block; tener años / tener frío is a daily trap

main.job: want (a thing or to do something)

main.why: the everyday must-job in Latin America; a separate job from tener (R-TERM-05)

main.job: go: movement to a place (ir a + place)
main.why: go-job building block; only the ir a + infinitivo future pattern is known, not movement (R-EX-03)
come-job building block; ir/venir perspective differs from English come/go

main.job: like: the thing liked is the subject (me gusta, te gustan)
main.why: unlocking construction; the reversed structure blocks talking about likes until learned

spares.why: the recent-past partner of the known ir a + infinitivo
softer obligation next to tener que

spares.job: know a fact / know how to do something

jobs_covered.negation: not claimed: no before the verb works like English 'not' and is assumed at A2
jobs_covered.questions: not claimed: intonation questions need no term; the question-word set (7+ members) is bigger than the remaining count, so it is not started (R-SEL-04)
jobs_covered.politeness / referring to people: not claimed: the tú / usted / ustedes set needs 3 slots and would push out spine verbs; not started (R-SEL-04)

shape.notes: bare slice, A2–B1. Excluded items are phrase-scope patterns, so estar and ir are selected for their own jobs. Every item is a building block or unlocking construction; no nouns, no greetings.
